records.source: וַיָּקָם֩ אַחֲרֵ֨י אֲבִימֶ֜לֶךְ לְהוֹשִׁ֣יעַ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל תּוֹלָ֧ע בֶּן־פּוּאָ֛ה בֶּן־דּוֹד֖וֹ אִ֣ישׁ יִשָּׂשכָ֑ר וְהֽוּא־יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּשָׁמִ֖יר בְּהַ֥ר אֶפְרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And arose after Abimelech to save Israel Tola son of Puah son of Dodo, [a] man of Issachar; and he [was] living in Shamir in [the] hill country of Ephraim.
pieces: After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He was a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.

L.1: And after Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar; and he was living in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.

R.1: After Abimelech died, a man named Tola came forward to save Israel. He was the son of Puah and the grandson of Dodo, from the tribe of Issachar. He lived in the town of Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.

decisions.choice: arose to save Israel: came forward as a rescuer
decisions.reason: The verb "save" is the one used of the judges the LORD raised up (2:16, 18; 3:9, 15). The text does not say whom Tola saved Israel from; after the ruin Abimelech brought on Shechem and Thebez (chapter 9), the rescue may have been from that disorder as much as from an outside enemy.

decisions.choice: Tola son of Puah, a man of Issachar: family names of Issachar
decisions.reason: Tola and Puah (also spelled Puvah) are the names of two of Issachar's sons (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:23; 1 Chronicles 7:1). This Tola carries old family names of his tribe.

decisions.choice: Dodo: a personal name
alternatives: son of Puah, son of his uncle
decisions.reason: The word is read as a name, as in 2 Samuel 23:9. The same letters could mean "his uncle", making Puah the uncle's son; the ancient Greek translation took it that way. As a list of fathers' names, a name fits best.

decisions.choice: a man of Issachar living in Shamir in Ephraim
decisions.reason: Issachar's land lay in the valley of Jezreel to the north (Joshua 19:17-23), but Tola lived in the hills of Ephraim, nearer the middle of the land. The site of Shamir is not known.

decisions.choice: Tola ... rose up / came forward; Readable "died", "grandson", "the town of"
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the subject first. Readable says what "after Abimelech" means (after his death, 9:54-55), that "son of Dodo" here means grandson, and that Shamir is a town.

records.heading: Tola and Jair

records.source: וַיִּשְׁפֹּט֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עֶשְׂרִ֥ים וְשָׁלֹ֖שׁ שָׁנָ֑ה וַיָּ֖מָת וַיִּקָּבֵ֥ר בְּשָׁמִֽיר׃פ
records.gloss: And he judged Israel twenty and three year[s], and he died and was buried in Shamir.
pieces: He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.

L.2: And he judged Israel twenty-three years, and he died and was buried in Shamir.

R.2: Tola led Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.

decisions.choice: judged Israel: led and governed Israel
decisions.reason: As at 2:16, a judge was a leader raised up to rescue Israel and govern it, more than a judge in a court.

decisions.choice: a short notice of a leader
decisions.reason: Tola and Jair (verses 3-5) are given only a few facts: where they came from, how long they led, and where they were buried. The same pattern returns for Ibzan, Elon and Abdon (12:8-15).

decisions.choice: led Israel
decisions.reason: As at 2:16: Readable says "led", since "judged" suggests only a court judge. Readable also names Tola as the subject.

records.source: וַיָּ֣קָם אַחֲרָ֔יו יָאִ֖יר הַגִּלְעָדִ֑י וַיִּשְׁפֹּט֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עֶשְׂרִ֥ים וּשְׁתַּ֖יִם שָׁנָֽה׃
records.gloss: And arose after him Jair the Gileadite, and he judged Israel twenty and two year[s].
pieces: After him came Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years.

L.3: And after him there arose Jair the Gileadite, and he judged Israel twenty-two years.

R.3: After Tola, a man named Jair came forward. He was from Gilead, and he led Israel for twenty-two years.

decisions.choice: Jair the Gileadite: from Gilead east of the Jordan
decisions.reason: Gilead was the hill country east of the Jordan, settled by Gad and half of Manasseh (Numbers 32:39-42). An earlier Jair of Manasseh had taken villages there and named them after himself (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14); this judge comes from the same region and bears the same name.

decisions.choice: led Israel; "He was from Gilead"
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, Readable says "led". It explains "the Gileadite" as "from Gilead".

records.source: וַֽיְהִי־ל֞וֹ שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים בָּנִ֗ים רֹֽכְבִים֙ עַל־שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים עֲיָרִ֔ים וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים עֲיָרִ֖ים לָהֶ֑ם לָהֶ֞ם יִקְרְא֣וּ׀חַוֺּ֣ת יָאִ֗יר עַ֚ד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּאֶ֥רֶץ הַגִּלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: And were to him thirty sons riding on thirty male donkeys, and thirty towns [were] to them; to them they call Havvoth-jair until the day this, which [are] in [the] land of Gilead.
pieces: Jair had thirty sons, riding thirty donkeys, and they owned thirty towns. Those towns in the land of Gilead are known as Havvoth-jair to this day.

L.4: And he had thirty sons riding on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty towns; they call them Havvoth-jair to this day, which [are] in the land of Gilead.

R.4: Jair had thirty sons, and each one rode his own donkey and had his own town. These thirty towns are in the land of Gilead, and to this day people call them Havvoth-jair, which means "Jair's villages."

decisions.choice: thirty donkeys ... thirty towns: a play on two words that sound alike
decisions.reason: The word for young male donkeys and the word for towns are written here with the same letters. The usual word for "towns" is a little different; it is spelled here to match "donkeys", so the line plays on the sound: thirty sons on thirty donkeys, with thirty towns.

decisions.choice: riding on donkeys: a mark of rank and wealth
decisions.reason: Leaders and their families rode donkeys (5:10; 12:14; 2 Samuel 16:2). Thirty sons each with his own mount and town show a large, wealthy household that governed a whole region.

decisions.choice: Havvoth-jair to this day: the villages of Jair
decisions.reason: The name means "the villages of Jair" or "Jair's tent villages". It is already given to villages in Gilead in Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14, and "to this day" shows that the narrator writes when the name was still in use.

decisions.choice: donkeys ... towns
decisions.reason: English has no pair of words that sound alike for donkeys and towns, so every level gives the plain sense, and a footnote points out the play on words. Readable adds what the name Havvoth-jair means and puts "each one" for the matching numbers.

records.gloss: And died Jair and was buried in Kamon.
pieces: Then Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

L.5: And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

R.5: Then Jair died and was buried in the town of Kamon.

decisions.choice: Kamon: a town in Gilead
decisions.reason: Kamon is mentioned only here. It most likely lay in Gilead, Jair's home region; its site is not certain.

records.source: וַיֹּסִ֣פוּ׀בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת הָרַע֮ בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָה֒ וַיַּעַבְד֣וּ אֶת־הַבְּעָלִ֣ים וְאֶת־הָעַשְׁתָּר֡וֹת וְאֶת־אֱלֹהֵ֣י אֲרָם֩ וְאֶת־אֱלֹהֵ֨י צִיד֜וֹן וְאֵ֣ת׀אֱלֹהֵ֣י מוֹאָ֗ב וְאֵת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י בְנֵי־עַמּ֔וֹן וְאֵ֖ת אֱלֹהֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּעַזְב֥וּ אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה וְלֹ֥א עֲבָדֽוּהוּ׃
records.gloss: And added [the] sons of Israel to do the evil in [the] eyes of Yahweh, and they served the Baals and the Ashtaroth and [the] gods of Aram and [the] gods of Sidon and [the] gods of Moab and [the] gods of [the] sons of Ammon and [the] gods of [the] Philistines; and they forsook Yahweh and not they served him.
pieces: Once again the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did what was evil in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. They served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and no longer served {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.6: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel again did the evil in [the] eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and they served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and the gods of Aram and the gods of Sidon and the gods of Moab and the gods of the sons of Ammon and the gods of the Philistines; and they forsook {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and did not serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.6: Once again the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said was evil. They worshiped the Baals and the goddesses called the Ashtaroth. They also worshiped the gods of the nations around them: Aram, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and Philistia. They turned away from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and stopped serving {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: again did the evil in the eyes of the LORD: began the cycle once more
decisions.reason: "Added to do" means did again. The words open each new turn of the cycle in Judges: Israel sins, the LORD hands them over to enemies, they cry out, and he raises a rescuer (2:11-19; 3:7, 12; 4:1; 6:1; 13:1). Evil "in his eyes" is evil as the LORD judges it.

decisions.choice: the Baals and the Ashtaroth: the gods and goddesses of Canaan
decisions.reason: Baal was the Canaanite storm god, worshiped under many local names, so the plural means the Baal gods of many places; Ashtaroth is the plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a goddess of love and war. Together they stand for the whole of Canaanite worship (2:13; 1 Samuel 7:4; 12:10).

decisions.choice: seven groups of gods: worship of every neighbor's gods
decisions.reason: The list names seven kinds of gods, from Canaan, Aram to the north, Sidon on the coast, Moab and Ammon to the east and the Philistines to the west. It is the longest such list in the book: Israel took up the gods of every people around them. The LORD's answer in verses 11-12 names seven peoples he had saved them from.

decisions.choice: forsook the LORD and did not serve him: worship of him given up
decisions.reason: The last clause does not only say they added other gods. It says they left the LORD and stopped serving him, as 2:12-13 also says.

decisions.choice: the Baals and the goddesses called the Ashtaroth
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the names and says who the Ashtaroth were, as in 2:13. It joins the lists of nations in two short sentences.

decisions.choice: abandoned ... no longer served
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "abandoned" for the older "forsook" kept at Literal, and the same word in verses 10 and 13 where the Hebrew repeats the verb.

records.heading: Israel cries out under the Ammonites

records.source: וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַֽיִּמְכְּרֵם֙ בְּיַד־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וּבְיַ֖ד בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And burned [the] anger of Yahweh against Israel, and he sold them into [the] hand of [the] Philistines and into [the] hand of [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: Then the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} blazed against Israel, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sold them into the power of the Philistines and into the power of the Ammonites.

L.7: And the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} burned against Israel, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sold them into [the] hand of the Philistines and into [the] hand of the sons of Ammon.

R.7: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} became very angry with Israel. He handed them over to the Philistines and the Ammonites.

decisions.choice: the anger burned: he was very angry
decisions.reason: Hebrew speaks of anger as burning or growing hot (2:14, 20; 3:8).

decisions.choice: sold them into the hand of: handed them over to the power of
decisions.reason: "Selling" people into an enemy's hand means giving them up to that enemy's control (2:14; 3:8; 4:2). The "hand" is power.

decisions.choice: the Philistines and the Ammonites: enemies on two sides
decisions.reason: The Philistines pressed on Israel from the coast in the west, the Ammonites from the east across the Jordan. The Ammonite threat is told first (10:8-12:7, Jephthah); the Philistine one comes later (chapters 13-16, Samson).

decisions.choice: handed them over to
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of selling into someone's hand, as in 3:8 and 4:2; Balanced keeps "sold ... into the power of".

records.source: וַֽיִּרְעֲצ֤וּ וַיְרֹֽצְצוּ֙ אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בַּשָּׁנָ֖ה הַהִ֑יא שְׁמֹנֶ֨ה עֶשְׂרֵ֜ה שָׁנָ֗ה אֶֽת־כָּל־בְּנֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ בְּעֵ֣בֶר הַיַּרְדֵּ֔ן בְּאֶ֥רֶץ הָאֱמֹרִ֖י אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּגִּלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: And they shattered and crushed [the] sons of Israel in the year that, eighteen year[s], all [the] sons of Israel who [were] across the Jordan in [the] land of the Amorite[s], which [is] in Gilead.
pieces: That year they shattered and crushed the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}, and for eighteen years they oppressed all the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} who lived east of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites.

L.8: And they shattered and crushed the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel in that year; for eighteen years [they did so to] all the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel who [were] across the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which [is] in Gilead.

R.8: That year they began to crush the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} and treat them harshly. For eighteen years they did this to all the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} who lived east of the Jordan River, in Gilead, where the Amorites used to live.

decisions.choice: shattered and crushed: two words of breaking, used together
decisions.reason: The two verbs sound alike and both mean to break or crush. Together they stress how hard the oppression was. The same pair describes the fate of a disobedient Israel in Deuteronomy 28:33.

decisions.choice: in that year ... eighteen years: it began that year and lasted eighteen
decisions.reason: The sentence is compressed: the attack began "in that year", and for eighteen years it went on against the Israelites east of the Jordan. The second part has no verb of its own; it takes its sense from the first.

decisions.choice: across the Jordan in the land of the Amorites in Gilead
decisions.reason: "Across the Jordan" is seen from the land west of the river, so it means east of it. This region had been the land of the Amorite king Sihon before Israel took it (Numbers 21:21-31), and it bordered Ammon.

decisions.choice: Literal "[they did so to]"; Balanced "they oppressed"; Readable "they did this to"
decisions.reason: English needs a verb for the second half of the sentence. Every level supplies one from the first half; Literal puts it in brackets. Readable says "used to live" because by now Israel held the land.

records.source: וַיַּעַבְר֤וּ בְנֵֽי־עַמּוֹן֙ אֶת־הַיַּרְדֵּ֔ן לְהִלָּחֵ֛ם גַּם־בִּיהוּדָ֥ה וּבְבִנְיָמִ֖ין וּבְבֵ֣ית אֶפְרָ֑יִם וַתֵּ֥צֶר לְיִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And crossed [the] sons of Ammon the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against [the] house of Ephraim; and it was distress to Israel greatly.
pieces: The Ammonites even crossed the Jordan to make war on Judah, on Benjamin and on the house of Ephraim. Israel was in great distress.

L.9: And the sons of Ammon crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim; and Israel was in great distress.

R.9: The Ammonites even crossed the Jordan River to fight against the tribes of Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim. Israel was in terrible trouble.

decisions.choice: Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim: the tribes west of the Jordan
decisions.reason: The Ammonites did not stop at Gilead. They crossed the river into the central and southern hill country, the heart of Israel's land.

decisions.choice: it was distress to Israel greatly: Israel was hard pressed
decisions.reason: The verb means to be tight or narrow, a picture of being hemmed in. It is used of Israel's trouble in 2:15.

decisions.choice: the tribes of; "even"
decisions.reason: Readable names these as tribes, and "even" shows that the attack had spread beyond the east side of the river.

records.source: וַֽיִּזְעֲקוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה לֵאמֹ֑ר חָטָ֣אנוּ לָ֔ךְ וְכִ֤י עָזַ֨בְנוּ֙ אֶת־אֱלֹהֵ֔ינוּ וַֽנַּעֲבֹ֖ד אֶת־הַבְּעָלִֽים׃פ
records.gloss: And cried out [the] sons of Israel to Yahweh, saying, we have sinned against you, and indeed we have forsaken our God and we have served the Baals.
pieces: Then the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: "We have sinned against {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, because we have abandoned our God and served the Baals."

L.10: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying, "We have sinned against {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, for we have forsaken our God and served the Baals."

R.10: Then the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for help. They said, "We have sinned against {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}. We turned away from {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, our God, and worshiped the Baals."

decisions.choice: cried out: the call for help that turns each cycle
decisions.reason: Israel's cry to the LORD comes at the low point of each cycle (3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:6-7). This time, for the first time in the book, the cry includes a confession of sin.

decisions.choice: and indeed we have forsaken: the confession names the sin
decisions.reason: The small word can mean "because" or simply stress what follows ("indeed"). Either way the second clause says what the sin was: leaving their own God for the Baals.

decisions.choice: for help; "you, our God"
decisions.reason: Readable says that the cry was a call for help. Since the people are speaking to the LORD, it says "turned away from you, our God", which keeps the sense of "forsaken our God".

records.source: וַ֥יֹּאמֶר יְהוָ֖ה אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל הֲלֹ֤א מִמִּצְרַ֨יִם֙ וּמִן־הָ֣אֱמֹרִ֔י וּמִן־בְּנֵ֥י עַמּ֖וֹן וּמִן־פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh to [the] sons of Israel, [did I] not from Egypt and from the Amorite[s] and from [the] sons of Ammon and from [the] Philistines
pieces: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites and the Philistines?

L.11: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, "[Did I] not [save you] from Egypt and from the Amorites and from the sons of Ammon and from the Philistines?

R.11: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} answered the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}, "Remember how I saved you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites and the Philistines.

decisions.choice: the question breaks off: "Did I not save you from ...?"
alternatives: read verses 11-12 as one long sentence: "Was it not from Egypt ... and the Sidonians ... oppressed you, and I saved you?"
decisions.reason: The Hebrew begins a question, "Was it not from Egypt and from the Amorites ...", and does not finish it; verse 12 goes on with more names and ends with "I saved you from their hand". The sense of the whole is "Did I not save you from all of these?" The broken sentence may show the force of the LORD's reply.

decisions.choice: Egypt, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines: past rescues
decisions.reason: Egypt recalls the exodus; the Amorites, Israel's victories over Sihon and Og (Numbers 21:21-35); the Ammonites, the war of Eglon king of Moab with Ammon at his side (3:13); the Philistines, Shamgar's victory (3:31).

decisions.choice: Literal "[Did I] not [save you]"; Balanced "Did I not save you"; Readable "Remember how I saved you"
decisions.reason: English cannot leave the question unfinished and still be clear, so every level supplies "save you" from verse 12; Literal puts the supplied words in brackets. Readable turns the question into the statement it expects.

records.source: וְצִידוֹנִ֤ים וַֽעֲמָלֵק֙ וּמָע֔וֹן לָחֲצ֖וּ אֶתְכֶ֑ם וַתִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֵלַ֔י וָאוֹשִׁ֥יעָה אֶתְכֶ֖ם מִיָּדָֽם׃
records.gloss: and [the] Sidonians and Amalek and Maon oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you from their hand.
pieces: When the Sidonians, the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I saved you from their power.

L.12: And the Sidonians and Amalek and Maon oppressed you, and you cried out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I saved you from their hand.

R.12: When the Sidonians, the Amalekites and the Maonites treated you cruelly, you cried out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I saved you from them.

decisions.choice: Maon
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text reads "Maon", a people of the south also named among Israel's enemies in 2 Chronicles 26:7 (Meunites). Many manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation read "Midian", which would recall Gideon's war (chapters 6-8). The Hebrew text is followed here.

decisions.choice: seven peoples: the LORD's record of rescue
decisions.reason: With verse 11 the LORD names seven peoples he saved Israel from, matching the seven groups of gods Israel served in verse 6. Not every one of these rescues is told in Judges; the list sums up the LORD's faithfulness against Israel's unfaithfulness.

decisions.choice: from their hand: from their power
decisions.reason: As in verse 7, the "hand" is the power of the enemy.

decisions.choice: the Amalekites and the Maonites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the peoples by the usual English forms for them; Literal keeps "Amalek" and "Maon" as the Hebrew has them.

records.source: וְאַתֶּם֙ עֲזַבְתֶּ֣ם אוֹתִ֔י וַתַּעַבְד֖וּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֑ים לָכֵ֥ן לֹֽא־אוֹסִ֖יף לְהוֹשִׁ֥יעַ אֶתְכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And you, you have forsaken me and you have served gods other; therefore not I will add to save you.
pieces: Yet you have abandoned {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and served other gods. So I will not save you again.

L.13: But you, you have forsaken {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and served other gods; therefore I will not again save you.

R.13: But you left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and worshiped other gods. So I will not save you anymore.

decisions.choice: and you, you: stress on Israel's part
decisions.reason: The extra word "you" sets Israel's conduct against what the LORD had done in verses 11-12: he saved, but they left him.

decisions.choice: I will not again save you: a real refusal, not the last word
decisions.reason: The LORD refuses to rescue them again, as a judgment on their repeated turning away. Verse 16 shows that the story does not end there, and 11:29-33 tells of the rescue that followed.

decisions.choice: will not add: will not do again
decisions.reason: The verb is the one that opened the cycle in verse 6: Israel "added" to do evil, and now the LORD will not "add" to save them.

records.source: לְכ֗וּ וְזַֽעֲקוּ֙ אֶל־הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּחַרְתֶּ֖ם בָּ֑ם הֵ֛מָּה יוֹשִׁ֥יעוּ לָכֶ֖ם בְּעֵ֥ת צָרַתְכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen them; they, let them save you in [the] time of your distress.
pieces: Go and cry to the gods you chose for yourselves. Let them be the ones to save you when trouble comes."

L.14: Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."

R.14: Go and cry out for help to the gods you chose! Let them save you from your trouble."

decisions.choice: go and cry out ... let them save you: a challenge with bitter irony
decisions.reason: The commands are not real instructions to pray to other gods. They show that those gods cannot help, since they had never saved Israel (compare Deuteronomy 32:37-38; Jeremiah 2:28).

decisions.choice: the gods you have chosen: worship as a choice
decisions.reason: Israel had once chosen to serve the LORD (Joshua 24:15, 22). Now the LORD says they have chosen other gods, and must face what that choice brings.

decisions.choice: cry out for help
decisions.reason: As in verse 10, Readable says that the cry is a call for help, and an exclamation mark gives the tone of the challenge.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֶל־יְהוָה֙ חָטָ֔אנוּ עֲשֵׂה־אַתָּ֣ה לָ֔נוּ כְּכָל־הַטּ֖וֹב בְּעֵינֶ֑יךָ אַ֛ךְ הַצִּילֵ֥נוּ נָ֖א הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And said [the] sons of Israel to Yahweh, we have sinned; do you to us according to all the good in your eyes; only rescue us please the day this.
pieces: But the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "We have sinned. Deal with us in whatever way {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} think best, but please rescue us today."

L.15: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "We have sinned. You do to us according to all that [is] good in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes; only rescue us, please, this day."

R.15: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "We have sinned. Do to us whatever {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} think is right. But please rescue us now!"

decisions.choice: we have sinned; do to us whatever is good in your eyes: submission to the LORD's judgment
decisions.reason: The people repeat their confession and accept whatever punishment the LORD chooses, as long as he rescues them from the enemy now. Compare David's words in 2 Samuel 24:14.

decisions.choice: rescue: snatch away from danger
decisions.reason: This verb is different from "save" in verses 12-14. It means to pull someone out of danger (6:9; 8:34).

decisions.choice: You do to us
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the pronoun that the Hebrew adds to the command. At the start of a sentence it is capitalized either way.

records.source: וַיָּסִ֜ירוּ אֶת־אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַנֵּכָר֙ מִקִּרְבָּ֔ם וַיַּעַבְד֖וּ אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה וַתִּקְצַ֥ר נַפְשׁ֖וֹ בַּעֲמַ֥ל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: And they removed [the] gods of the foreignness from their midst, and they served Yahweh; and was short his soul with [the] misery of Israel.
pieces: Then they got rid of the foreign gods that were among them and served {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could bear Israel's misery no longer.

L.16: And they removed the foreign gods from among them and served {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} soul became short with the misery of Israel.

R.16: So the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} got rid of the foreign gods they had and worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} again. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} could not stand to see Israel suffer any longer.

decisions.choice: removed the foreign gods: turning back to the LORD in deed
decisions.reason: Putting away foreign gods is the act of returning to the LORD, as Jacob's household did (Genesis 35:2-4) and as Joshua urged (Joshua 24:23; compare 1 Samuel 7:3-4). Israel now acts on its confession.

decisions.choice: his soul became short with the misery of Israel: he could no longer bear their suffering
alternatives: he grew impatient with the trouble of Israel
decisions.reason: A "short soul" means not being able to hold out any longer (Numbers 21:4; Judges 16:16). Here the LORD can no longer bear to watch Israel's misery, and so he is moved to act. Some read it the other way: he grew impatient with Israel and its troubles. But after the people's turning back, the sense of compassion fits best, and the word for misery is used of suffering under hardship (Deuteronomy 26:7).

decisions.choice: the LORD's feelings described in human terms
decisions.reason: The text speaks of the LORD's inner self being moved, as it speaks of his anger in verse 7 and his pity in 2:18. It does not say that he promised to save them; the rescue comes through Jephthah (11:29-33).

decisions.choice: could bear ... no longer / could not stand to see ... suffer
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable explain the idiom instead of keeping the picture of a "short soul", which in English would mean nothing. Readable names the subject again, "the LORD", so that it is clear who could not stand it, and adds "again", since Israel had served the LORD before.

records.source: וַיִּצָּֽעֲקוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בַּגִּלְעָ֑ד וַיֵּאָֽסְפוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בַּמִּצְפָּֽה׃
records.gloss: And were summoned [the] sons of Ammon and they encamped in Gilead; and gathered [the] sons of Israel and they encamped at Mizpah.
pieces: When the Ammonites were called to arms, they made camp in Gilead, while the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} came together and made camp at Mizpah.

L.17: And the sons of Ammon were called out, and they camped in Gilead; and the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel gathered, and they camped at Mizpah.

R.17: The Ammonite army was called together, and it camped in Gilead. The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} gathered too, and they camped at Mizpah.

decisions.choice: were called out: were summoned for war
decisions.reason: The verb is the same one used for Israel "crying out" (verse 12), here in a form that means being called up to fight (7:23-24; 12:1). While Israel cried to the LORD, Ammon was called to arms.

decisions.choice: Mizpah: a gathering place in Gilead
decisions.reason: The name means "lookout". This is the Mizpah of Gilead where Jacob and Laban set up a heap of stones (Genesis 31:49), and Jephthah's home (11:11, 34), not the Mizpah in Benjamin (20:1).

decisions.choice: called to arms / the Ammonite army was called together
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the summons was for.

records.heading: Gilead looks for a leader

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ הָעָ֜ם שָׂרֵ֤י גִלְעָד֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֔הוּ מִ֣י הָאִ֔ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָחֵ֔ל לְהִלָּחֵ֖ם בִּבְנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן יִֽהְיֶ֣ה לְרֹ֔אשׁ לְכֹ֖ל יֹשְׁבֵ֥י גִלְעָֽד׃פ
records.gloss: And said the people, [the] princes of Gilead, each to his neighbor, who [is] the man who will begin to fight against [the] sons of Ammon? he will be for head to all [the] inhabitants of Gilead.
pieces: The people and the officials of Gilead asked one another, "Who will be the man to open the fight against the Ammonites? He will be head over everyone who lives in Gilead."

L.18: And the people, the princes of Gilead, said, each to his neighbor, "Who [is] the man who will begin to fight against the sons of Ammon? He will be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."

R.18: The people and the leaders of Gilead said to each other, "Who will lead the attack on the Ammonites? That man will become chief over everyone who lives in Gilead."

decisions.choice: the people, the princes of Gilead: the people with their leaders
alternatives: the people's leaders, the princes of Gilead
decisions.reason: The two phrases stand side by side with no "and". They may mean "the people, that is, the leaders", the leaders speaking for the people; or the people and their leaders together. The leaders are the ones who later make the offer to Jephthah (11:5-11).

decisions.choice: will begin to fight: will lead the first attack
decisions.reason: To "begin" the fight is to take the lead in it, going first against the enemy (compare 1:1-2).

decisions.choice: head: the leader of the whole region
decisions.reason: "Head" means a leader over a people, more than a war leader. This is the offer that the elders of Gilead later make to Jephthah, who asks for it in full (11:8-11).

decisions.choice: Literal "princes", Balanced "officials", Readable "leaders"; "to one another"
decisions.reason: As for the officials of Succoth (8:6, 14): these are the chief men of the clans of Gilead. "Each to his neighbor", kept at Literal, is the Hebrew way of saying "to one another".

decisions.choice: chief
decisions.reason: Readable uses "chief", a plain word, for "head", so that it is not confused with leading the attack.
